title: Teaching Grit
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Note traces grit from its Old English roots as gravel to its modern sense of sustained passion and perseverance toward long-term goals. It draws on Angela Duckworth's research to argue that grit isn't just a trait to screen for in candidates but a capacity leaders can actively build. The mechanism is Duckworth's Hard Thing Rule: a daily practice outside one's comfort zone that demands sustained effort and honest feedback. The piece walks through why such practice is uncomfortable and why that discomfort is precisely what builds character. It closes by putting the coaching responsibility on leaders: help people choose a hard thing, set realistic but difficult goals, and track milestones.
points: Grit historically meant gravel, evoking an abrasive, persistent way of pushing through difficulty.
Duckworth's Hard Thing Rule -- a daily practice outside one's comfort zone -- is the mechanism for building grit.
Gritty practice requires managing frustration and sacrificing time and comfort for long-term mastery.
Leaders build grit in others by helping them choose a hard thing, set goals, and track milestones.
The range of viable 'hard things' is nearly limitless, from weightlifting to language learning.
quotes: Since the late 16th century, the word has been used to refer to a strength of human character, denoting pluckiness and tenacity.
Gritty people work strenuously toward challenges and maintain a constant effort despite setbacks and moments of failure.
The Hard Thing Rule is the daily practice of something outside your comfort zone.
They give up time, energy, and resources for the kind of practice that is uncomfortable and takes away from more pleasurable pursuits.
They promote the idea that the stubborn refusal to quit is a cardinal virtue.
The end result is a tad more Grit. Enduring the uncomfortable for a larger purpose is something people can learn if done in everyday practice.
